title: 496. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Converse Inverse and Contrapositive
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Form the converse of a conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the converse of \(p\implies q\)?
questions.explanation: The converse exchanges the hypothesis and the conclusion: \(q\implies p\). The statement \(\neg q\implies\neg p\) exchanges and negates both parts; it is the contrapositive.
questions.hint: The converse swaps the two parts without negating them.

questions.learningObjective: Form the contrapositive of a conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the contrapositive of \(p\implies q\)?
questions.explanation:
The contrapositive exchanges the hypothesis and the conclusion and negates both: \(
eg q\implies
eg p\). The statement \(
eg p\implies
eg q\) negates both parts without exchanging them; it is the inverse.
questions.hint: The contrapositive both swaps and negates.

questions.learningObjective: Form the inverse of a conditional statement.
questions.question: What is the inverse of \(p\implies q\)?
questions.explanation: The inverse negates the hypothesis and the conclusion while keeping their order: \(\neg p\implies\neg q\). The statement \(q\implies p\) is the converse, which exchanges the parts without negating them.
questions.hint: The inverse negates both parts but does not swap them.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the related conditional that is logically equivalent to the original.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional \(p\implies q\)?
questions.explanation:
The conditional \(p\implies q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. The contrapositive \(
eg q\implies
eg p\) is false only when \(
eg q\) is true and \(
eg p\) is false, which is the same situation. The converse is false in a different row, when \(q\) is true and \(p\) is false.
questions.hint: Find the single row in which each statement is false.

questions.learningObjective: Write the converse of a conditional about divisibility.
questions.question: What is the converse of "If an integer is divisible by \(6\), then it is divisible by \(3\)"?

options.label: A
options.text: "If an integer is not divisible by \(3\), then it is not divisible by \(6\)."

options.label: B
options.text: "If an integer is divisible by \(3\), then it is divisible by \(6\)."

questions.explanation: The converse exchanges the hypothesis and the conclusion, giving "If an integer is divisible by \(3\), then it is divisible by \(6\)". The other sentence exchanges and negates both parts, so it is the contrapositive.
questions.hint: Swap the "if" part and the "then" part without adding negations.

questions.learningObjective: Write the contrapositive of a conditional involving inequalities.
questions.question: For a real number \(x\), what is the contrapositive of "If \(x>2\), then \(x^2>4\)"?
questions.explanation: The contrapositive negates both parts and exchanges them. The negation of \(x^2>4\) is \(x^2\le 4\), and the negation of \(x>2\) is \(x\le 2\), giving "If \(x^2\le 4\), then \(x\le 2\)". The other sentence only exchanges the parts, so it is the converse; it is false for \(x=-3\).
questions.hint: Negate both inequalities and swap their positions.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether the converse of a true conditional is true.
questions.question: The statement "If an integer is divisible by \(6\), then it is divisible by \(3\)" is true. Is its converse true?

options.label: A
options.text: No; \(3\) is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(6\).

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; the converse of a true statement is always true.

questions.explanation: The converse is "If an integer is divisible by \(3\), then it is divisible by \(6\)". The integer \(3\) satisfies the hypothesis but not the conclusion, so the converse is false. A conditional and its converse are not logically equivalent, so the truth of one says nothing about the other.
questions.hint: Look for an integer divisible by \(3\) that is not divisible by \(6\).

questions.concept: Equivalent pair among the related conditionals
questions.learningObjective: Identify which two of the converse, inverse, and contrapositive are equivalent to each other.
questions.question: Which two statements are logically equivalent to each other?

options.label: A
options.text: The converse and the contrapositive of a conditional

options.label: B
options.text: The converse and the inverse of a conditional

questions.explanation:
The converse is \(q\implies p\) and the inverse is \(
eg p\implies
eg q\). The inverse is the contrapositive of the converse, so these two are equivalent. The contrapositive \(
eg q\implies
eg p\) is equivalent to the original conditional, not to the converse.
questions.hint: Take the contrapositive of the converse and see which statement appears.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether the inverse of a true geometric conditional is true.
questions.question: The statement "If a quadrilateral is a square, then it is a rectangle" is true. Is its inverse true?

options.label: A
options.text: No; a rectangle with sides \(2\) and \(3\) is not a square, but it is a rectangle.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; negating both parts of a true statement gives a true statement.

questions.explanation: The inverse is "If a quadrilateral is not a square, then it is not a rectangle". A rectangle with unequal sides satisfies the hypothesis (it is not a square) but violates the conclusion (it is a rectangle). So the inverse is false. The inverse is equivalent to the converse, not to the original statement.
questions.hint: Find a quadrilateral that is not a square but is still a rectangle.

questions.learningObjective: Write the contrapositive of a conditional whose conclusion is a disjunction.
questions.question: For real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), what is the contrapositive of "If \(ab=0\), then \(a=0\) or \(b=0\)"?
questions.explanation:
The contrapositive negates both parts and exchanges them. By De Morgan's law, the negation of "\(a=0\) or \(b=0\)" is "\(a
e 0\) and \(b
e 0\)", and the negation of \(ab=0\) is \(ab
e 0\). The version with "or" is false: for \(a=1\) and \(b=0\) its hypothesis holds, but \(ab=0\).
